concept_title: Scalar Product and Work Done by Constant Force
next_video_title: Work Done by Variable Force & F-x Graph Area
ncert_citation: NCERT Class 11 Physics Part 1, Chapter 5, Section 5.2 - 5.3
ncert_core_rule: Work is a scalar quantity equal to the dot product of force and displacement vectors. Work is zero if displacement is zero, force is zero, or angle is 90 degrees.
author_book_nuance: Centripetal force and normal force on a horizontal surface do zero work because theta = 90 degrees (cos 90 = 0).
neet_trap_point: Confusing the sign of work: work is negative when theta > 90 degrees (e.g. friction opposing displacement).
chapter_core_topics: Work Done, Work-Energy Theorem, Kinetic Energy

subject: Physics
concept_title: Work Done by Variable Force and Area Under F-x Curve
next_video_title: Kinetic Energy & Work-Energy Theorem for Variable Force
latex_formula: W = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x) \, dx = \text{Area under } F\text{-}x \text{ curve}
plain_formula: W = integral(F(x) dx) = Area under F-x curve
ncert_citation: NCERT Class 11 Physics Part 1, Chapter 5, Section 5.4 - 5.5
ncert_core_rule: Work done by a position-dependent force is the definite integral of F with respect to x, geometrically represented by the signed area between the F-x curve and position axis.
author_book_nuance: Areas below the displacement axis represent negative work done and must be subtracted algebraically from areas above.
neet_trap_point: Adding negative area under position axis as positive magnitude instead of subtracting signed integral value.
chapter_core_topics: Variable Force Work, F-x Area, Integration

subject: Physics
concept_title: Work-Energy Theorem for Constant & Variable Forces
next_video_title: Conservative vs Non-Conservative Forces & Path Independence
latex_formula: W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = K_f - K_i = \frac{1}{2}m v_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}m v_i^2
ncert_citation: NCERT Class 11 Physics Part 1, Chapter 5, Section 5.3 & 5.5
ncert_core_rule: The net work done by all forces (conservative, non-conservative, internal, and external) on a particle equals the change in its kinetic energy.
author_book_nuance: Work-energy theorem is valid in non-inertial frames provided the work done by pseudo forces is also included in W_net.
neet_trap_point: Considering only conservative forces in work-energy theorem; W_net includes friction, normal, tension, and applied forces.
chapter_core_topics: Work-Energy Theorem, Delta K, Net Work

subject: Physics
concept_title: Conservative vs Non-Conservative Forces and Path Independence
next_video_title: Potential Energy & Conservative Force Relation F = -dU/dx
ncert_citation: NCERT Class 11 Physics Part 1, Chapter 5, Section 5.6
ncert_core_rule: A force is conservative if work done around any closed loop is zero, or equivalently, work done between two points depends only on end points and is independent of path.
author_book_nuance: Gravity, electrostatic, and spring forces are conservative. Friction, air resistance, and viscous drag are non-conservative (dissipative).
neet_trap_point: Assuming friction work is zero in a round trip; friction always opposes instantaneous displacement, so W_friction < 0 over a closed loop.
chapter_core_topics: Conservative Forces, Path Independence, Closed Loop Zero Work

subject: Physics
concept_title: Potential Energy and Force Relation F = -dU/dx
next_video_title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy & Free Fall Conversion
ncert_citation: NCERT Class 11 Physics Part 1, Chapter 5, Section 5.6 - 5.7
ncert_core_rule: Potential energy is defined only for conservative forces. The conservative force is the negative spatial gradient of the potential energy function.
author_book_nuance: Equilibrium occurs where dU/dx = 0 (stable if d2U/dx2 > 0, unstable if d2U/dx2 < 0, neutral if d2U/dx2 = 0).
neet_trap_point: Forgetting the negative sign in F = -dU/dx, which leads to inverting force direction and misidentifying equilibrium stability.
chapter_core_topics: Potential Energy Gradient, F = -dU/dx, Equilibrium Stability

subject: Physics
concept_title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy in Free Fall & Pendulums
next_video_title: Hooke's Law & Elastic Potential Energy of Ideal Spring
latex_formula: E = K + U = \text{constant}, \quad K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f
plain_formula: E = K + U = constant, K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f
ncert_citation: NCERT Class 11 Physics Part 1, Chapter 5, Section 5.7
ncert_core_rule: In an isolated system with only conservative internal forces doing work, total mechanical energy (sum of kinetic and potential energy) remains constant.
author_book_nuance: In free fall from height h, at any height y: 0.5*m*v^2 + m*g*y = m*g*h = constant; velocity at bottom is v = sqrt(2gh).
neet_trap_point: Applying mechanical energy conservation when non-conservative forces like friction or air drag do non-zero work.
chapter_core_topics: Mechanical Energy Conservation, Free Fall, K + U = E

subject: Physics
concept_title: Hooke's Law and Elastic Potential Energy of an Ideal Spring
latex_formula: F_s = -k x, \quad U_s = \frac{1}{2} k x^2, \quad W_s = -\frac{1}{2}k(x_f^2 - x_i^2)
ncert_citation: NCERT Class 11 Physics Part 1, Chapter 5, Section 5.8
ncert_core_rule: The restoring force of an ideal massless spring obeys Hooke's Law F_s = -k*x. The stored elastic potential energy is U_s = 0.5*k*x^2, which is always positive for both extension and compression.
author_book_nuance: Work done by the spring is W_s = -Delta U_s = 0.5*k*(x_i^2 - x_f^2). When extended from equilibrium x=0 to x_m, W_s = -0.5*k*x_m^2.
neet_trap_point: Thinking spring potential energy is negative during compression: U_s is proportional to x^2, so it is strictly positive whether extended or compressed.

subject: Physics
concept_title: Vertical Spring-Mass Dynamics and Maximum Extension
ncert_citation: NCERT Class 11 Physics Part 1, Chapter 5, Section 5.8 - 5.9
ncert_core_rule: When a mass m is released from rest from an unstretched vertical spring, energy conservation m*g*x = 0.5*k*x^2 yields maximum extension x_max = 2mg/k, exactly twice the static equilibrium extension x_eq = mg/k.
author_book_nuance: Maximum speed occurs at the equilibrium position x_eq = mg/k where net force is zero, NOT at maximum extension where velocity drops to zero.
neet_trap_point: Confusing equilibrium extension x_eq = mg/k with maximum dynamic extension x_max = 2mg/k.
chapter_core_topics: Vertical Spring, x_eq = mg/k, x_max = 2mg/k, Maximum Speed

subject: Physics
concept_title: One-Dimensional Elastic Collisions and Head-On Impact
next_video_title: Inelastic Collisions, Coefficient of Restitution & Kinetic Loss
ncert_citation: NCERT Class 11 Physics Part 1, Chapter 5, Section 5.12
ncert_core_rule: In an elastic collision, both total linear momentum and total kinetic energy are strictly conserved. For identical masses (m1 = m2), colliding bodies completely exchange their velocities.
author_book_nuance: Relative velocity of approach equals relative velocity of separation: u1 - u2 = v2 - v1 (coefficient of restitution e = 1).
neet_trap_point: Applying velocity exchange formula when masses are unequal; velocity exchange occurs ONLY when m1 = m2.
chapter_core_topics: Elastic Collisions, Momentum Conservation, Velocity Exchange

subject: Physics
concept_title: Inelastic Collisions, Coefficient of Restitution and Kinetic Energy Loss
next_video_title: Average & Instantaneous Power and Force-Velocity Relation
ncert_citation: NCERT Class 11 Physics Part 1, Chapter 5, Section 5.12.2
ncert_core_rule: In an inelastic collision (0 <= e < 1), total momentum is conserved but kinetic energy decreases as it converts to heat/sound/deformation. In a completely inelastic collision (e = 0), colliding bodies stick together with maximum fractional kinetic energy loss.
author_book_nuance: Common velocity for completely inelastic collision: v = (m1*u1 + m2*u2) / (m1 + m2).
neet_trap_point: Believing momentum is lost in an inelastic collision: momentum is strictly conserved in all collisions where F_ext = 0; only kinetic energy is lost.
chapter_core_topics: Inelastic Collision, Coefficient of Restitution e, Kinetic Loss

subject: Physics
concept_title: Instantaneous Power, Average Power, and Force-Velocity Relation
latex_formula: P = \frac{dW}{dt} = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v} = F v \cos\theta, \quad P_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta W}{\Delta t}
plain_formula: P = dW/dt = F * v * cos(theta), P_avg = Delta W / Delta t
ncert_citation: NCERT Class 11 Physics Part 1, Chapter 5, Section 5.11
ncert_core_rule: Power is the time rate at which work is done or energy is transferred. Instantaneous power is the scalar dot product of force vector and instantaneous velocity vector: P = F . v.
author_book_nuance: For a machine delivering constant power P, acceleration decreases as speed increases: a = P / (m * v); velocity scales as v proportional to t^(1/2) and distance s proportional to t^(3/2).
neet_trap_point: Confusing constant power with constant force: constant power implies non-constant force and non-uniform acceleration (v proportional to sqrt(t), not t).
chapter_core_topics: Instantaneous Power, P = F . v, Constant Power Motion
